summary: Williams sits in the Sacramento Valley about 65 miles northwest of Sacramento, and the number that jumps off the page is a median home value of roughly $340,000 against a median household income north of $93,000 — a price-to-income ratio near 3.6, which is remarkably accessible by California standards and almost unheard of anywhere within a couple hours of the Bay Area. The town is flat, agricultural, and honest about what it is: a small grid of streets along Interstate 5, surrounded by almond orchards, rice fields, and the wide-open sky of the northern Central Valley. Summers are emphatically hot, with average daily highs pushing well into the upper 80s and 90s and nearly 9.4 hours of sunshine per day year-round, while winter nights dip into the 40s with tule fog rolling off the fields. Employment is overwhelmingly tied to agriculture and the logistics corridor along I-5; switching jobs without a commute to Colusa, Woodland, or Sacramento is a real constraint. The property crime rate — particularly larceny at over 1,086 per 100,000 — is elevated for a town this small, worth weighing against the affordability. Williams is the kind of place where a $340,000 mortgage is genuinely attainable on a local salary, but the tradeoff is that almost everything beyond groceries and gas requires a drive.
